tldr: By sharing a tactile sensor layout and aligning action spaces between human hands and a multi-fingered robot hand, the authors built a high-accuracy world model that learns from 100 hours of human manipulation data to predict future visual and tactile changes on the robot.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of DexTouch-WM. On the left, an anatomy-aware tokenizer encodes bilateral tactile maps. On the right, a pretrained video model and a tactile expert interact via joint attention to jointly predict future video frames and tactile residuals.
overview:
In dexterous robot manipulation, contact dynamics—such as pressure shifts and slips when fingers touch an object—make or break task success. Camera images alone cannot reveal contact states hidden behind fingers, so existing video world models struggle to simulate contact accurately. At the same time, collecting large volumes of tactile data via real-robot teleoperation is prohibitively slow and expensive.

To solve this, the authors asked: if we align the tactile sensor layout and action spaces between humans and robots, could we train a robot world model using human manipulation data? They attached piezoresistive sensor arrays with an identical layout to both human gloves and a 20-DoF dexterous robot hand. Retargeting human hand motions into the robot's joint space created a shared interface that processes human and robot data under the same framework.

The proposed method, DexTouch-WM, combines an anatomy-aware tactile tokenizer, residual prediction anchored to initial contact states, and dual-rate action conditioning to bridge time resolutions between video and touch, coupling a Wan2.2 video foundation model with a tactile expert. Keeping real-robot supervision fixed at just 5 hours while scaling human interaction data up to 100 hours substantially boosted visual, geometric, and contact prediction accuracy on unseen robot tasks. Furthermore, the learned world model was shown to serve both as a surrogate simulation environment for policy evaluation and as a synthetic data generator for policy learning.
contributions: Enabled training of robot future prediction from human tactile manipulation data using a shared flexible tactile sensor layout and aligned action representations across humans and robots.

Proposed a world model architecture featuring an anatomy-aware tactile tokenizer, residual prediction anchored to initial contact, and dual-rate action conditioning matched to video and tactile sampling frequencies.
Constructed HumanTouch, a 100-hour bimanual manipulation dataset, demonstrating that adding human data alone improves prediction accuracy in robot environments without increasing robot data.
Demonstrated that the learned tactile world model functions both as an offline policy evaluator and as a synthetic trajectory generator for imitation learning.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of Tactile Learning and World Models: From Human Hands to Robots
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work in tactile policy learning, human data utilization, and visual-tactile world models. The key differentiator of this study is its focus on action-conditioned transfer of contact dynamics from humans to robots.
sections.details:
In tactile manipulation learning, prior studies have fused camera images with contact feedback to govern delicate grasps or transferred tactile policies across different sensors and robots (such as FTP-1 and TactAlign). Collecting visual-tactile data from humans using sensorized gloves has also been explored (such as OpenTouch and DexUMI), but those efforts mainly targeted imitation learning or representation learning, not learning predictive models of future contact dynamics.

In visual-tactile world modeling, works like VT-WM and ViTacWorld have addressed future prediction and planning conditioned on contact dynamics. However, most rely heavily on real-robot teleoperation data, remain restricted to parallel grippers or a few fingertip sensors, and face hurdles when scaling to dense, multi-fingered hand contacts.

DexTouch-WM bridges these two fields. By deploying dense tactile arrays covering the entire hand alongside a shared human-robot interface, it explores a new paradigm: scaling a multi-fingered robot world model using rich contact interaction data gathered on the human body.

sections.heading: The Full Method: Anatomy-Aware Tactile Tokenizer and a Shared Interface
sections.summary: This section details DexTouch-WM's inputs and outputs, its model architecture coupling video and touch, and the data pipeline unifying human and robot sensing and actions. Residual prediction from the initial state and dual-rate conditioning are key to its accuracy.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation
The model inputs are an initial RGB image $\mathbf{v}_0$, initial bilateral tactile maps $\mathbf{x}_0$, a language instruction $\ell$, and a sequence of future hand poses $\mathbf{a}_{1:T}$. From these, it models the joint distribution of future video frames $\mathbf{v}_{1:T}$ and bilateral tactile maps $\mathbf{x}_{1:T}$. Human hand movements are retargeted into the robot joint space and unified into a 67-dimensional pose representation covering bimanual wrist poses, 20-DoF finger joint angles, and head camera movement.

### III-B Action-Conditioned Tactile World Models
The backbone uses the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B video diffusion model (DiT) and video VAE, coupled with a lightweight tactile expert. Built on a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) structure, it interchanges visual and tactile information via masked bidirectional joint attention at each layer, while computing feedforward networks independently for each modality.

Three core design choices are crucial:
- **Anatomy-Aware Tactile Tokenizer (Split-Hands)**: Flattening 320 tactile sensing elements per hand (five $4\times 4$ fingertips, one $15\times 16$ palm) into a single 2D image introduces false spatial adjacencies between distant fingertips. Instead, separate encoders are used for fingertips and palms, tagged with Pad Identity Embeddings.
- **Residual Prediction Anchored to Initial State**: Rather than predicting raw tactile values directly, the model predicts the residual $\Delta\mathbf{z}_t$ relative to initial tactile features $\mathbf{z}_0$. This prevents the model from being biased by resting contact pressures and focuses its capacity on contact onset, release, and pressure variations caused by motion.
- **Dual-Rate Action Conditioning**: While the causal video VAE compresses time by $4\times$, the tactile expert preserves high frame-by-frame temporal resolution. Using AdaLN, 4-frame pooled poses are injected into the video side while per-frame poses are fed into the tactile side, resolving the temporal rate mismatch.
Training is performed with Conditional Flow Matching, weighting tactile losses toward contact-active regions and changing tokens.

### III-C Human Data Collection Pipeline (HumanTouch)
Participants wore piezoresistive tactile gloves (using 320 of 360 elements per hand) overlaid with Manus MetaGloves, while HTC Vive trackers captured 6-DoF wrist poses. Synchronizing head and wrist cameras, they recorded 100 hours across 50 everyday tasks, including transport, picking, handoffs, collisions, insertions, and deformable object manipulation.

### III-D Human-to-Robot Action Alignment
Recorded human wrist poses and 25-keypoint hand skeletons are mapped via inverse kinematics (IK) onto the kinematics of the robot hand (WujiHand2). Combined with the identical sensor layout on the robot, this allows human motion data to serve directly as training supervision for the robot world model.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: 100 Hours of Human Data Unlock Prediction Accuracy and New Uses
sections.summary: Scaling experiments keeping 5 hours of robot data fixed while varying human data from 0 to 100 hours show marked gains in visual and tactile prediction accuracy. The authors also validate its utility as a policy evaluation simulator and a data generator for imitation learning.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Architecture Ablations
Controlled experiments were conducted using only the 5 hours of robot data.
First, evaluating tactile representations: comparing "Grid" (processing the entire hand as a single image via CNN) against "Split-Hands" (separating fingertips and palm), Split-Hands achieved significantly lower reconstruction loss and converged much faster on Contact-IoU.
Next, action conditioning was compared. Combining video and touch with Cross-Attention caused interference, lowering Trajectory Accuracy from 0.88 to 0.85. In contrast, AdaLN (Robot-only) restored Trajectory Accuracy to 0.89 while improving tactile Contact-IoU from 0.39 to 0.42 and Contact-F1 from 0.52 to 0.55.

### IV-C Scaling with Scalable Human Interaction
With robot data fixed at 5 hours, human interaction data was scaled from 0 hours (Robot-only) to 10, 50, and 100 hours (DexTouch-WM). Evaluation was performed on 6 held-out robot tasks that did not overlap with human tasks.
Adding 100 hours of human data raised visual PSNR from 23.47 to 27.10, boosted Trajectory Accuracy from 0.89 to 0.96, and reduced Geometry Error from 0.13 to 0.10. Tactile improvements were even more pronounced: Contact-IoU jumped from 0.42 to 0.59, and Contact-F1 rose from 0.55 to 0.71. While visual metrics showed signs of saturation around 50 hours, contact prediction continued to improve steadily through 100 hours, proving that human data serves as a highly effective scaling axis for contact dynamics.

### IV-D World Models as Surrogate Environments for Policy Evaluation
Real-robot policies (FTP-1, $\pi_{0.5}$, X-VLA) were run closed-loop inside the learned world models to assess how well their success scores and rankings matched real-world evaluations. Compared to "WM-Robot" (adapted on robot data alone), "WM-Mix" (replacing half the robot data with human task data) raised the Pearson correlation with real evaluations from 0.646 to 0.844 and reduced rank reversals (MMRV) from 0.025 to 0.017. Mixing in human data yielded an evaluation simulator much closer to the physical robot.

### IV-E World Models as Synthetic Trajectory Generators for Policy Learning
Visual-tactile synthetic trajectories produced by the world model were used to train real-robot policies. Although generated trajectories closely mirrored real data in visuals and contact timing, their impact on policy learning varied by model. For FTP-1, mixing synthetic data remained competitive (0.694) compared to real-only data (0.731). However, performance dropped for $\pi_{0.5}$ and X-VLA. This highlights an important challenge: even when a world model excels at policy evaluation, its effectiveness as a training data generator depends heavily on downstream policy characteristics.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: This work demonstrates that shared tactile sensor layouts and action alignment allow visual-tactile robot world models to learn from human manipulation. Human interaction data offers a promising, scalable alternative to real-robot teleoperation.
sections.details:
This paper presented DexTouch-WM, an action-conditioned tactile world model leveraging shared human-robot sensing and action space alignment. Combining just 5 hours of real-robot data with 100 hours of human daily manipulation data significantly boosted visual, geometric, and contact prediction accuracy on unseen robot tasks.

Furthermore, the learned world model proved to be an effective offline policy evaluator with strong real-world correlation, and for certain policies, functioned as a supplementary data generator for imitation learning. Rather than depending on expensive, hard-to-scale real-robot teleoperation, gathering data from humans wearing tactile sensors represents an important step toward foundation models for dexterous robot manipulation.

takeaways: Aligning tactile sensor layouts and hand action spaces between humans and multi-fingered robots enables direct transfer of human contact interaction data to robot dynamics learning.
When handling hand tactile data, anatomically separating fingertips from the palm and predicting residuals relative to initial contact are decisive factors for high accuracy.
While video prediction saturates at moderate data volumes, contact state prediction continues to improve steadily all the way to 100 hours of human data, offering strong scaling returns.
High world model quality and effective policy evaluation do not automatically guarantee success when using generated rollouts as training data for imitation learning.
limitations: Physical differences in hand compliance, friction coefficients, and kinematic link structures between humans and robots are not fully compensated.
Policy learning on synthetic rollouts generated by the world model suffered performance drops on certain policy architectures, falling short of fully replacing real-robot data.
Wearing and calibrating tactile glove hardware still requires a specialized physical setup.
